Words come out of every mouth that can speak. Some people call them tools, some call them weapons, and the ones who like to sound clever call them power. There is one thing said about them that everyone seems to know: once a word is said, it can't be taken back. I think most people mean that as a warning about cruelty, about the things you shout in an argument and regret in the morning. I understood it that way too, for most of my life. I'm not sure when I stopped. Probably on the night I'm about to tell, though it may have been later, once I'd had time to go over it.

A word leaves your mouth, and after that it belongs to the world. If it comes true, nobody remembers you said it. If it doesn't, it comes back to you. That is what I believed, anyway. I believed it for a long time.

I was sitting on the floor of the hallway outside our bedroom with my back against the wall. My hands were red, and I remember thinking, slowly, that the blood wasn't mine, though some of it was. The white marble had long dark lines across it. Angie was a few feet from me, on her side in her pink pajamas, and her eyes were open.

Somewhere outside, sirens were coming closer.

Why did I say that?

3 hours and 47 minutes earlier

"You're going to ruin your eyes," I said.

Angie didn't look up from the book. She had the lamp tilted toward her side of the bed and her knees pulled up under the blanket, the book resting against them. It was a thick paperback with a cracked spine. She'd bought it secondhand from a stall near the old bus station, and somebody else's name was written inside the cover in blue ink.

"I said I'd finish it this week," she said.

"You said that on Sunday."

"And this is still the week." She turned a page. "I keep my promises."

She did, mostly. It was one of the first things I had noticed about her, years before, when she promised a friend's little brother she would come to his school play and then sat through two hours of it in the back row, clapping for every single entrance. She made promises easily, to anyone, about anything. She had promised the basil plant on the kitchen windowsill that it would live, though it had come home from the market already yellow at the edges. She watered it every morning and talked to it while the kettle boiled. Three days in, it was still yellow, but it hadn't died.

We had been married for three days.

"Angie," I said. "It's past midnight."

She folded down the corner of her page and closed the book on her finger. She didn't switch the lamp off.

"I don't really want to sleep," she said.

"The dreams again?"

She nodded. She had mentioned them twice since the wedding and once before it. She never described them properly. She said it was a feeling more than a story, that something in the house was wrong and she was the only one who knew it.

"It's a new house," I said. "That's all it is. You're not used to the sounds yet."

"Maybe." She looked at the door, then back at me. "It's stupid."

"It isn't stupid."

I sat up and moved closer to her. I put my hand on her face, and she held it there against her cheek with both of hers and closed her eyes. Her hands were warm from the lamp. We stayed like that for a while. I could hear the fridge humming in the kitchen and a dog somewhere down the street.

"Say something," she said, without opening her eyes. "Something I can sleep on."

I didn't think about it. I didn't need to.

"I won't let anything happen to you," I said, "as long as I am beside you."

She opened her eyes and looked at me for a second, as if she was checking the words for cracks and hadn't found any. Then she smiled.

"Okay," she said.

She switched off the lamp. In the dark she put the book on the bedside table, moved in against my shoulder and found my hand under the blanket. Her breathing slowed long before mine did. I remember lying there feeling pleased with myself. I had said the right thing, and it had worked.

3 hours later

The sound was glass, a lot of it, and close.

We were both awake at once. Angie's hand was still in mine, and it closed hard around my fingers. Neither of us moved. I could hear my own heart, and then hers, or maybe it was only mine twice.

"Stay here," I whispered.

She took hold of my shirt with her other hand.

"It's probably nothing," I said. "Something fell. Stay here."

She let go of my shirt slowly, one finger at a time, as if she had to make each one do it.

I went to the wardrobe and knelt in the dark. On the bottom shelf, behind two pairs of shoes, there was a white box. I had bought the gun inside it a year before the wedding, after a break-in two streets away, and I had never fired it anywhere but a range. I took it out. When I turned around, Angie was sitting up in bed, looking at it, then at me.

I lifted my free hand, palm down, and lowered it slowly. It's nothing. It's only in case.

The hallway was dark. I didn't turn on the light, because I thought whoever it was shouldn't know where I was. I think that was my reason. I've gone over it enough times that I can't be sure anymore which reasons I had then and which I've added since.

The kitchen door was half open, and cold air was coming through it. I stepped forward, felt glass under my bare foot, and then something hit the back of my head, hard, and the floor came up at me.

I don't know how long I was down. Not long. A few seconds, maybe. I remember the tiles against my cheek, and that my hand was empty.

Then I heard Angie say my name, in the hallway. She hadn't stayed.

There was a sound I had only ever heard at a range, much louder inside a house. A short silence. Then footsteps, fast, going past me. I was crawling by then, toward the hallway, toward her. I had got as far as the doorframe when the second shot hit me in the back and pushed me flat.

The footsteps went out through the kitchen and over the broken glass, and then there was nothing.

It took me a long time to reach her. I don't know how long. Something was wrong with my legs, and the floor kept tilting. When I got there I took her hand, and it was still warm, and I held on to it.

I didn't cry, not then. I sat with my back against the wall and her hand in mine, and I looked at the wall opposite, which was white and had a small scuff mark near the skirting board that I had been meaning to paint over. I looked at that mark for a long time. Everything seemed to be happening a little after it happened, as if there was a lag between me and the rest of the world.

Her hand was getting colder. I held it tighter, as if that would help.

I won't let anything happen to you as long as I am beside you.

The sirens were close now. Blue light was moving on the ceiling at the far end of the hallway.

I had been beside her. That was the part I kept coming back to, then and afterward. I had been right there.

3 years later

The doctors took the bullet out of my back the first night and told me afterward that I had been lucky. I said, "Yes." It was true. A little to the left, they said, and I wouldn't have walked again. I walked out of the hospital after five weeks. I still feel it when it's going to rain, a dull pull low on the right side, like a thumb pressing there.

The police asked me what happened many times. I told them what I knew: the glass, the blow, two shots, the footsteps. I didn't tell them what I had said in bed three hours before. It didn't seem like something they could use. They never found him. They found my gun eleven days later, in a storm drain two streets away.

I went back to work after four months. I stayed in the house. I never painted over the scuff mark.

"Coming to Peter's farewell tonight?" Martin from accounts asked me that morning, leaning over the partition with his coffee.

"It's at six," I said. "In the conference room."

He waited a moment, in case there was more. There wasn't. He nodded and went back to his desk. People at the office had learned to stop waiting, mostly. I think they found me strange but reliable, the way you find a lift reliable. You press the button and it comes. You don't expect it to tell you anything.

At eleven the phone on my boss's desk buzzed, and I heard him through the glass. "Please send in Mr. Jacob."

His office was decent. A carpet that didn't match the chairs, a framed certificate, a plant someone else watered. He had a stack of files in front of him and he pushed them toward me as I sat down.

"Jacob, these are from the Airwave Parking project. A few of them were never checked. Go through them and confirm everything's still in order. I don't want anything coming back at us in six months."

I reached for the files and looked at him.

He kept his hand on them. "I need you to tell me you've understood and you're up for it. If you're not, I'll give them to someone else. That's fine. But you have to at least try to convince me. That's how this works."

"I can look at them," I said.

"Can," he said. "Not will."

I didn't say anything. I was looking at the files, not at him.

"Sir, I…" I stopped. "There's no… guarantee. In anything." My voice had gone quiet, the way it did. "Words, they… come back. I'd rather not."

He looked at me for a long moment. Then he got up, came around the desk and put his hand on my shoulder. It was heavier than I expected.

"Jacob, you're good at what you do. I don't want to watch you go down like this. Words, you say. Words are how we say what we want, and what we want says who we are. Wouldn't you agree?"

He waited. I tried to give him a nod. I think I managed half of one.

"I know what happened to you," he said, more quietly now. "We all do. I was at the funeral, Jacob. I stood at the back. But it's been three years, and at some point you have to start living again. If you're this scared of what you say, that fear is going to get into everything. It already has. Look, if something doesn't happen the way your words said it would, that doesn't make you a liar. It simply…"

"Means you didn't… mean them," I said, to the files. It came out smaller than I meant it to.

I didn't look up. I hoped my face was saying thank you for trying, and also it's late for this. I don't know what it actually said.

He took his hand off my shoulder. He took the files back, gently, the way you'd take scissors from a child. Then he went to his drawer, found a card, and slid it into the pocket of my shirt.

"You can go now," he said.

So I went.

I forgot about the card until it came out of the washing machine two weeks later, soft and grey, the corners curled. The print had survived. Dr. Sal. Clinical Psychologist. A phone number, an address above a pharmacy on Fourth Street.

I called it, I think, because it had survived the wash. That isn't a reason. It was what I had.

The office was on the third floor, up a staircase that smelled of cough syrup. There was a fish tank in the corner with one fat orange fish in it, and two armchairs that didn't match each other either. The man who opened the door was younger than I'd expected, with rolled-up sleeves and a mug that said YOU ARE THE BEST SATSU.

"Sal," he said, and shook my hand. "Just Sal. I'd like it if you used it."

"Doctor," I said.

He laughed, not unkindly. "We'll work on it."

In the first session I told him about the night. All of it, in order, with the times. The book, the lamp, the glass, the white box, the two shots, the scuff mark. I didn't leave anything out, including what I had said. It took about twenty minutes. Sal didn't write anything down. When I finished, he was quiet for a while, looking at the fish.

"You've told that before," he said.

"To the police. Eleven times."

"It doesn't seem to cost you much."

"The past is…" I stopped, and started again. "It's done. Nothing I say about it can… change it." I looked at the fish for a while. "Now is different. Now, what I say can still… come back."

He nodded slowly, as if I'd said something he'd need to think about. I think he did think about it. He was like that.

I went every Thursday at four. Sal tried things. He gave me sentences to finish. He asked me to describe what I would do next summer, and I told him what I had done last summer. He asked whether I'd come to the next session and I said, "It's in my calendar." He made tea that was always too strong and apologised for it every time and never made it weaker.

One Thursday in the second month he leaned forward before I could stand up.

"Humour me," he said. "When you leave today, just say see you next week. That's all. Three words."

I put on my coat. I went to the door and opened it. I stood there with my hand on the handle.

"My next appointment is Thursday at four," I said.

"That's not what I asked you to say."

"It's true," I said, to the door handle.

He smiled. "It is," he said, and let me go.

Another time, when I had gone over the night again, the way I sometimes did without being asked, the way you press on a bruise, he said, "You keep going back there as if it might come out different. Surfing the past won't make the waves of the present any smoother, Jacob. They'll still hit you."

"I know."

"Do you?"

I didn't answer that, because I didn't know.

Once, near the end of the second month, he said something else, and then never said it again.

"You've told me that night a lot of times, Jacob. You always tell me what you said." He turned his mug round on the arm of the chair. "You've never once told me whose gun it was."

I looked at the fish until the session was over.

In the third month he put his pen down at the start of a session, which he had never done, and looked at me with his elbows on his knees.

"I'm going to be honest with you," he said, "because I think you'd prefer it. I'm not helping you."

"No," I said.

He laughed out loud. "You could have hesitated a little. For my sake."

Then he told me about Hollis House. He volunteered there on Saturdays, a children's home on the edge of the city with a day centre attached. There was a boy there, nine years old, called Sana. He could hear perfectly well. He couldn't speak. He had never spoken. He used sign language, which he had mostly taught himself from a library book older than he was, and there was one woman on the staff who could sign back a little, when she had time, which was not often.

"He needs someone to sign with," Sal said.

"I don't know sign language."

"Neither did he."

"I can talk," I said. "He can hear me. Why would I need…"

"Signs?"

I nodded.

Sal leaned back in his armchair and looked very pleased with himself, the way he did whenever I asked a question instead of answering one. "You'll know," he said.

"That's not an answer."

"It's a better one than I've got." He shrugged. "The past you can talk about all day. It's the words about now, and about later, that you can't get out. Maybe answering those in a different way, for a while, could help you with them. I'd like to see if it does."

I looked at the fish. It was opening and closing its mouth at the glass.

"I'm not…" I said, and stopped there. I didn't know how that sentence ended, so I left it.

"You don't have to promise him anything," Sal said. "Just go."

I didn't say I would. He wrote the address on the back of another card and held it out, and I took it, and I put it in the same shirt pocket as the first.

You'll know. I thought about it on the bus home, and that night, and the next morning at my desk with the Airwave files open in front of me. It annoyed me. It was the kind of sentence I would never say, because there was no way to be sure of it, and Sal had said it as if it cost him nothing.

On Saturday I went.

Hollis House was a long brick building on the edge of the city, with a tin-roofed laundry shed at the back and a green iron gate at the front that didn't close properly. You had to lift it a little on its hinges and push. I learned that on the first day, after standing there for about a minute with my hand on it, thinking I had been locked out. That would have been an answer of a kind.

Mrs. Ilse met me in the hall. She was in her sixties, small, with a cardigan buttoned wrong and a ring of keys on a shoelace around her wrist. She told me she had worked at Hollis House for thirty-one years before she told me anything else.

"Sal's friend," she said.

"I'm one of his patients."

She looked at me over her glasses. "Well. That's honest." She started walking, and I followed her down a corridor with children's paintings taped along it at a child's height. "He'll be in the laundry shed. He goes there when it's loud. I'll tell you what I tell everyone, and you'll nod, and then you'll do what everyone does."

"What do you tell everyone?"

"Don't say you'll come back." She stopped at the back door with her hand flat on it. "People come here to feel good about themselves. That's all right. I don't mind it. But they say see you next week and I'll come on Sunday, and then they don't, and I'm the one who has to explain it. He's had enough people coming on Sunday."

I didn't nod. I didn't say anything either.

She waited for the nod. When it didn't come, she looked at me properly for the first time. Then she pushed the door open. "Well," she said again. "We'll see."

He was sitting on an upturned crate just inside the shed, between two machines that thumped. A thin boy, small for nine, with hair someone had cut with kitchen scissors and ears that went pink in the cold. He had a notebook on his knees, a school exercise book with a cardboard cover held together with brown tape, and a pencil so short he held it by the very end, with three fingers.

Mrs. Ilse signed something to him, slowly. I saw her point at me. He looked up, at my face and then at my hands, which were in my pockets, and went back to the notebook.

"That's him being polite," said Mrs. Ilse, and left us.

I sat on the other crate. I had brought a book from the library, Signing for Beginners, with a photograph on the cover of a smiling woman making a shape I couldn't read. I opened it at page one. Hello: a flat hand at the temple, moving outward, like a salute. I did it. He didn't look up. I did it again. The machines thumped.

I stayed an hour. When I left, I didn't say anything. I couldn't think of anything to say that was true except goodbye, and I didn't say that either. I lifted the gate on its hinges and pushed.

The next day I went back.

I couldn't have said why, not in a way I would have trusted. But I had noticed something on the bus home. For the whole hour in the shed, nobody had waited for me to say anything. Not the machines, and not the boy. When Mrs. Ilse pointed at me, he had looked at my hands, not my mouth.

On Monday I asked my boss if I could leave at half past three. He signed the form without asking why. He looked, for a moment, like a man who had been told something he'd been waiting to hear.

For the first week he didn't sign to me at all. I sat on my crate and worked through the book, and he drew, and I watched him without looking like I was watching. He drew the machines. He drew a sparrow that came to the doorway for crumbs, and the crumbs. He drew Mrs. Ilse's keys. At lunch he went across to the kitchen, and through the window I saw that when the cook put his plate down he touched his fingertips to his chin and brought his hand forward and down, toward her. Thank you. She never looked up from the pot. He did it every day anyway.

When the older boys came through the yard, he changed. His hands came in close to his chest and got small, and if he signed at all he signed almost inside his jacket. When they had gone, his hands came out again.

On the sixth day, I think it was the sixth, he left the notebook open on the crate when he went to lunch. I didn't touch it. But I could see the page. It was the very back, the inside of the cardboard cover, and there was a list on it in pencil. Names, though some of them weren't names exactly. Man with red car. The student lady. Mr. Kemal. Christmas people. Beside each one was a small number. 2. 3. 1. 3. 2. The highest number on the page was 4.

At the bottom, in the same careful slanting hand, was Jacob, and beside it a 6. Around the 6 the paper was grey and soft, where the numbers before it had been rubbed out.

I was back on my crate before he came in. He picked up the notebook, closed it, and didn't look at me.

The next day, when I arrived, I watched him open the notebook to the back, rub out the 6 with the end of his pencil, and write a 7.

On the bus home I thought about Mr. Kemal, who had come once.

In the second week I knew perhaps sixty signs, the way a tourist knows a language: nouns, numbers, please. On the Wednesday I spelled my name for him, letter by letter, J-A-C-O-B, getting the C wrong. He watched my hand the whole way through without any expression at all.

Then he put the pencil down. He pointed at me. He lifted his right hand and pressed the palm flat over his own mouth, closed, and held it there.

Mrs. Ilse was crossing the yard with a basket of sheets. She stopped in the doorway.

"Oh," she said. "He's given you a name."

"What does it mean?"

"It's a name sign. You get one from somebody who's been watching you. It's what they think you are." She shifted the basket on her hip. "He doesn't do it for everybody. He hasn't done one for me."

"But what does it mean?" I said again.

She looked at the boy's hand, still over his mouth, then at me. "I think you know better than I do," she said, and went on across the yard.

Sana took his hand down. He picked up the pencil and went back to his drawing.

I didn't argue with it. That evening I stood in front of the bathroom mirror and did it myself, my own palm over my own mouth, and looked at a man with his hand over his mouth.

A few days later the sparrow came back to the doorway, and Sana signed something to it, three quick signs, before it flew off. I didn't know any of them. That night I sat at the kitchen table with the library book until one in the morning, looking for them. I found two.

That Saturday Sal was in the yard, in a tracksuit that didn't fit him, being chased by about eight children and a football. I was in the shed doorway with Sana, getting again wrong for the fourth time. Sal saw us. He didn't come over. He stopped running just long enough to point at me, then tap the side of his own head, and mouth something across the yard. I couldn't hear it. I knew what it was anyway. Then a boy half his height took the ball off him, and he went after it, shouting that it was a foul.

Sana had a sign for rain that wasn't the real one.

The real one, Mrs. Ilse showed me later, is both hands coming down with the fingers loose, like water falling. Sana's started the same way, then stopped halfway, and his fingers tapped against the back of his other hand, quick and uneven. I watched him do it three times before I understood. It was rain on the tin roof of the laundry shed.

He had others. Bread was a flat palm held under his nose, and his eyes closing. A kite was one finger drawn up through the air, then a sudden jerk, then the whole hand opening. The cook's soup was two fingers stirring and then a hand on the stomach, patted twice. I think he had made perhaps forty of them. He never told me the number. I counted them later in the notebook, where he had drawn each one in pencil, with small arrows showing which way the hands should go.

I learned the real signs first, because he made me. He would sign something and wait, then take my wrists and move my hands into the right shape when I got it wrong. His fingers were always cold. Mine were always too stiff. Again, he would sign, a bent hand tapping the flat of the other palm, and I would do it again.

It was easier than speaking. I noticed that in the second week and didn't mention it to Sal. A sign takes time to make. You can see it forming in front of you, and stop it if you want to. A spoken word is out before you hear it.

On a Tuesday, I think it was a Tuesday, he opened the notebook to a page I hadn't seen. It was a list in a careful, slanting hand, one word to a line. RAIN. BREAD. MINE. MOTHER. GREEN. More went on underneath, down past the fold.

He put his finger under the first one and looked at me.

I signed rain, the real one.

He shook his head. He pointed at my mouth, then at the word, then at my mouth again.

A boy was shouting in the corridor, and somebody was dragging a chair. Sana waited. He didn't sign please. He just kept his finger under the word, as if it might move.

"Rain," I said.

It came out too quietly, almost nothing. He frowned, then got up on his knees on the crate and put two fingers flat against the side of my throat, the way a doctor checks for a pulse.

Again, he signed with his other hand.

"Rain."

He kept his fingers there after the word had finished. I could feel them, cold, just under my jaw. He was looking at the wall behind me, listening with his hand.

Then he took his fingers away, made a small tick beside the word, and closed the notebook.

When I was leaving, I went past the shed window. He was still on the crate. His lips were moving, slowly, the same shape over and over, and two fingers of his own hand were pressed against his own throat.

After that, the last thing before I left was always one word. BREAD, on a Thursday. GREEN. KITE. MINE, which he made me say twice, and held his fingers there a long time afterward. Each one got its tick.

He skipped MOTHER. I noticed he skipped it, and I didn't ask.

The first time I heard Sana laugh, there was nothing to hear.

It was in the kitchen. I had decided to thank the cook myself, the way he did, and I made the sign with great care and complete confidence. The cook stared at me. Sana put both hands over his face, and his shoulders started to shake, and his mouth came open, wide, and stayed open, and no sound came out of it at all. When he could, he took my hand and corrected it. I had been telling her, very politely, that I needed the toilet.

He laughed about it for two days. Every time he saw the cook he looked at me, and his shoulders went.

He also cheated at games. He taught me one with bottle caps on the crate between us, a game whose rules changed whenever I started to understand them. The first time I won anyway, by accident, he swept every cap onto the floor and walked out of the shed. Ten minutes later he was back. He set the caps out on the crate again, signed again, and won, because he had made up a new rule on the way back.

It was in the yard that the other thing happened, in the second month, on a grey afternoon when he had taken me out to the bench by the wall to show me kite properly, with room for the hand to fly. Three older boys came round the side of the building. The tallest was called Victor. He was thirteen or so, with a shaved head and a laugh like a car that won't start. The other two laughed when he laughed.

Sana's hands came down and in, close to his chest. Victor had already seen the notebook on the bench. He picked it up, quick, as if it were his, and flipped through it.

"What's this, then?" He found the page. He read it in a high, breathy voice, like someone pretending to be a ghost. "Rain." The others laughed. "Bread. Mine. Mine! It's mine!"

Then he got to the fourth word. He said it in a baby's voice. "Mo-ther. Mo-ther, come back. Mo-ther." The other two picked it up and sang it, back and forth between them. "Mo-ther. Mo-ther."

Sana didn't move toward them. He stood with his arms down at his sides. His face didn't do anything. It was his hands I watched. They were shut so tight the knuckles had gone yellow.

"Give it back," I said.

It came out flat. There was nothing uncertain in it. It wasn't a promise. It was only a fact, and facts I could still say. Victor looked at me, then past me at the kitchen window, where Mrs. Ilse had stopped with her arms full of sheets. He held the notebook out. I took it. The three of them went back round the building, and one of them sang it once more on the way, quieter, "Mo-ther," and then they were gone.

I gave Sana the notebook. He held it against his chest with both arms. Then he looked up at me.

I knew the look. I had seen it once before, by lamplight, on a woman sitting up in bed with her hand on my shirt. It was the look of someone waiting for the next thing you say.

They won't do it again. Four words. I had the signs for them by then. I had both. My mouth opened. My hands came up a little way.

Nothing came out of either.

Sana's hands had started to rise; he had been going to sign something, and I will never know what. They went back down. Then, with the notebook held against him, he turned and walked to the laundry shed and sat on his crate with his back to the door.

That night in my kitchen I stood at the windowsill where the basil had been. The pot was still there. I had never thrown it out. There was only dry soil in it now.

"They won't," I said, out loud, to nobody.

I didn't say the rest.

I went back the next day anyway. I wanted to see whether his hands would come up again.

The next day Mrs. Ilse found me in the corridor. "Victor's been doing that since Sana was five," she said. "He does it because Sana can't shout back. I've told him off a hundred times. Telling is all I've got."

"Did Sana ever do anything?"

"Once. He threw a chair." She turned her keys around her wrist. "Then he stopped doing that too."

She told me about the third at the same time, I think because it was on her mind. "Don't come on the third," she said. "He won't be any use to you. He sits at the gate all day."

"Why the third?"

"That's the day he was left. Third of March, nine years ago. On the step, by the gate, in a blanket, with a note pinned to it." She shook her head. "Every month since he could walk. Doesn't matter if it's raining."

I went on the third.

He was on the low wall beside the gate, his coat buttoned up to his chin and the notebook on his knees, watching the road. I sat down beside him, not close enough to touch. Neither of us looked at the other, and neither of us signed.

We sat for an hour like that. Cars went past. A bus. A woman went by pushing a pram, and his head turned with her, slowly, all the way, until she was round the corner and gone, and then it turned back to the road. I didn't tell him she would come. I didn't tell him she wouldn't. I sat on the wall.

After a while he opened the notebook. Inside the front cover there was a plastic sleeve, the kind you keep a bus pass in, and inside that was a small piece of lined paper, folded into quarters and gone soft as cloth along the folds. He took it out and gave it to me.

It was one line in blue ballpoint, the letters leaning forward as if they were in a hurry.

I'll come back for you.

No name. In one corner there was a brown mark that could have been tea.

I gave it back to him. He folded it along the old lines and put it in the sleeve.

She comes, he signed. One day.

He looked at me then, but not as though he expected me to agree. More as if he was used to grown-ups not answering this one and was letting me off. He went back to the road.

Then, without turning his head, he signed again. You. Sad. Why?

He had asked before, two or three times. Each time I had pointed at the library book, or signed work, which was the sign I had learned earliest and used most.

I looked at my hands. I didn't have most of the signs. I spelled it, A-N-G-I-E, slowly. Then I clasped my hands together, the sign the book gave for married. Sana watched.

Night, I signed. Man came. Gun.

I made the gun with my hand and then I couldn't do anything with it. My hand stayed like that, two fingers out and the thumb up, for a few seconds, before I could put it down on my knee.

I started again. She was afraid. I said…

There wasn't a sign for it in my book, or if there was I hadn't got that far. I spelled it to him with my eyebrows up, the way the book said you ask a question. P-R-O-M-I-S-E?

Sana showed me. He touched one finger to his lips. Then he brought his flat hand down onto the palm of the other and pressed it there, as if he had taken the word out of his mouth and set it down and was holding it in place.

I asked him, with my eyebrows, to do it again. He did.

Then I did it. Finger to the lips. Hand down onto the palm. I promise. Nothing happens to you. I am here.

She died, I signed. I was there.

My hands were shaking by then so that the signs came out blurred. I did there three times before it was clear. Sana didn't look at the road once while I was doing it.

When I had finished, he reached across and took my hand, the right one, the one I'd been signing with, and held it on the wall between us. His fingers were cold. He didn't sign anything. Nobody had held my hand since the night I held Angie's.

We sat there until the streetlights came on. No one came up the road for him. At half past six Mrs. Ilse came out with a torch and said, "In, both of you," and we went in.

About a week later, when I was leaving, he followed me out to the gate, which he had never done before. I had lifted the gate on its hinges and was halfway through when he tapped my arm.

Tomorrow, he signed. You come?

His eyebrows were up. A question. It was the first time he had asked me anything about tomorrow.

My hands stayed at my sides. A bus went past behind me. I could feel the cold iron of the gate against my hip.

Then I lifted my hands, palms up, and moved them up and down, one and then the other, like a pair of scales weighing two things. Maybe.

It was the only word I had.

Sana watched my hands go up and down. Then he nodded, once, as if that was an answer, and went back inside. Through the hall window I saw him sit down on the bench and open the notebook at the back.

Angie died on the eleventh of December. Every year since, I had spent that day in the hallway.

I never planned it. The first year I woke up and found myself there by nine in the morning, sitting where I had sat, with my back against the same wall, looking at the scuff mark. The second year and the third, I didn't wake up surprised. I knew where I would be.

The fourth year was the same. I sat down at eight. Angie's book was on the shelf in the bedroom, where one of the policemen had put it back, with the corner of page 211 still folded down. I hadn't taken it off the shelf in four years. I didn't that day either.

At four in the afternoon the phone rang in the kitchen. Four was when I usually lifted the gate. It rang eleven times and stopped. At five it rang again. I stayed where I was.

At eleven at night I called Sal. Not the office. The other number, the one written on the back of the second card in his own handwriting.

He answered on the fifth ring, his voice thick with sleep. "If this is about my car's extended warranty," he said, "I'm not interested."

I didn't say anything. He waited. I heard him sit up, and the click of a lamp.

"Jacob," he said. It wasn't a question.

"It's the eleventh."

"I know what day it is."

"I didn't go."

He didn't ask where. "Okay."

"He'll have waited," I said. "I never told him I'd come. Not once. I never said it."

There was a long breath on the line. I thought he was going to explain something to me, and I waited for it. He didn't.

"Go tomorrow," he said.

"And tell him what?"

"You don't have to tell him anything," Sal said. "Go tomorrow."

Mrs. Ilse was standing in the hall when I came in, with her arms folded. It was the first time I had seen her without her keys turning round her wrist.

"He waited at the gate," she said. "From four o'clock until it was dark. It wasn't the third."

I didn't say anything.

"I rang you. Twice." She looked at me, and her face wasn't angry. It was only tired. "I told you on the first day. I told you not to promise him."

"I didn't," I said.

"No," she said. "You didn't."

She stepped aside and let me past.

He was on his crate in the laundry shed with his back to the door. He didn't turn round. The notebook was lying on the other crate, my crate, closed.

I opened it at the back.

Man with red car, 2. The student lady, 3. Mr. Kemal, 1. Christmas people, 3. All the names with their numbers, the way they had been on the sixth day.

At the bottom, Jacob. Nothing beside it.

The paper next to my name was worn grey and thin, almost through, where a long run of numbers had been rubbed out one after another. The last of them had been rubbed out too. I tilted the page toward the light from the doorway and could just make out its shape, pressed into the paper by the pencil: 31. After that, nothing. No 32. No 33.

I counted back. The thirty-first time I had come was the third of the month. The day at the gate.

I closed the notebook and put it back on the crate exactly where it had been.

He didn't sign to me that day. I sat on my crate for an hour, and he sat on his with his back to me, and the machines thumped, and that was all. When I left, I made the sign for sorry, a fist turning in a circle on the chest, to the back of his head. He didn't see it. I think he knew I'd made it, but he didn't see it.

The next day, when I came into the yard, he got up from the bench and went to the other side of it. The day after that he was in the shed again, but with his hands in his pockets, where I couldn't have read them even if he had used them.

On the third night I took Angie's book down from the shelf.

I said I'd finish it this week. That had been four years ago. I didn't know how long a week was allowed to be.

It was lighter than I remembered. I opened the cover. The other person's name was still there in blue ink. Angie had never written her own. I turned to page 211, where the corner was folded, and saw that I didn't know what the book was about. I had never asked her. It was about a postman in a mountain village who kept delivering letters to a house where nobody lived anymore.

I couldn't sign to a back. For three days I had made signs at the back of his head, and they had gone nowhere, because a sign needs someone to look at it. A voice doesn't. A voice goes round the back of a head and in, whether you turn or not. It was also the one thing he had ever asked me for.

The next afternoon I sat down on my crate in the laundry shed, with Sana's back to me, and opened the book at the fold, and started reading it out loud.

My voice was wrong. It hadn't gone further than a sentence at a time in four years, and it didn't know how. It came out thin, and it stopped at commas where there weren't any. I read about the postman climbing the path in the snow. I read about the dog that followed him halfway every morning and then sat down and waited for him to come back. On page 214 the postman's sister put the kettle on, and my voice broke on kettle, which is not a word anybody's voice should break on. I stopped. I started the sentence again.

I didn't know if he was listening. On page 216 the postman stood at the door of the empty house with a letter in his hand and knocked anyway, though he knew nobody would answer. He did it every morning. Nobody in the village told him to stop, and nobody told him to keep going. I read that page twice without meaning to. Then the dog was sitting halfway up the path again, waiting for him to come back down, and I thought of the low wall by the gate, and I had to start the sentence over.

Somewhere around page 220, Sana turned sideways on his crate.

I kept reading. I didn't look at him. By page 226 he was facing me, with his knees pulled up and his arms around them. The light in the doorway went from white to yellow. Once, Mrs. Ilse's shadow came across the floor and stood there for a while and then went away again.

Around page 230 he got up. He came across the shed and knelt up on my crate beside me, and he put two fingers flat against the side of my throat, the way he did after every word, except that this time I didn't stop. I kept going. He kept his fingers there. My voice broke three or four more times after that, on nothing words, on the and gate and Thursday, and each time I felt him feel it, and I went on.

It took an hour and forty minutes to get to the end. The postman went up the mountain again on the last page, in the morning, with the letters in his bag, though nobody had answered any of them.

I closed the book. My throat hurt.

Sana took his fingers away. He sat back on his heels and looked at me. Then he pointed at me, and put his palm flat over his own mouth, the way he had in the second week. He held it there.

Then he opened it. Slowly, outward, away from his lips, the fingers spreading as they went, the way you'd let something go that you'd been carrying in your hand.

He did it twice, to make sure I had seen.

I called Sal from the bus stop outside Hollis House. It was the office number this time, the middle of the afternoon, and he picked up on the first ring.

"Sal," I said. "How do I adopt a child?"

There was a silence. Then: "Say that again."

"How do I adopt a…"

"No," he said. "The first part."

I stood at the bus stop with the phone against my ear. The woman next to me was trying to fold a pushchair with one hand.

"Sal," I said.

He laughed. Then he put his hand over the phone for a while, and when he came back his voice was rough, and he said he would make some calls.

It took seven months. There were forms, and then forms about the forms. A social worker came to the house and opened every cupboard in my kitchen and stopped at the empty pot on the windowsill, and wrote something down. The week after, I put a basil plant in it. It was the last one at the market and it was already yellow at the edges. I watered it every morning.

The week before he came, I painted the hallway. White again, the same white. I did the mark last. After the first coat I could still see it, faint, a grey smudge near the skirting board, like something under ice. I stood there with the brush in my hand and told Angie, out loud, to the empty hallway, that a boy was coming. It was the first thing I had said to her in four years.

I didn't do a second coat.

Mrs. Ilse wrote my reference. She gave me a copy in an envelope. It was two typed pages of the proper things, and at the bottom, under her signature, in pen, it said: He comes.

At the panel, a man with a grey moustache read from a sheet without looking up. "Mr. Jacob, can you commit to caring for this child until he is an adult?"

"Yes," I said.

He wrote it down and went on to the next question.

It was during the forms that I asked Mrs. Ilse about the name. She told me there had been an older boy at Hollis House when Sana was small, a Spanish boy called Mateo, who had decided the baby needed a better name than the one on the register. Mateo said Sana was Latin for sound. A sound nobody else could hear, he said. That was why the baby didn't make any. Sana's sign for his own name was a cupped hand beside his ear, shaken very gently, as if there was something in it.

I looked it up that night. I didn't tell anyone what I found.

He left Hollis House on a Saturday in July. He had a blue sports bag with everything he owned in it, and the notebook under his arm. Mrs. Ilse stood on the step with her keys going round and round her wrist. Sal came, because he said he wanted to see it with his own eyes, and he shook Sana's hand and then made the sign for hello, very badly, a salute that went off sideways. Sana laughed with his shoulders, and corrected him.

At the gate he stopped.

He looked at the step, and at the low wall, and at the road going away in both directions. I didn't hurry him. A car went past. Then another one. He watched them go.

Then he turned round and held out the notebook, open at the very last page.

I had never seen that page. It had always been folded over and held down with a paperclip. The paperclip was gone. There was one word on it, in the careful slanting hand, larger than the others and pressed so hard the pencil had gone shiny.

STAY.

There was no tick beside it.

He pointed at the word. Then he pointed at my mouth.

"Stay," I said.

He got up on his toes and put two fingers against my throat. I said it again, so he could feel it. Then he took the pencil from behind his ear and made the tick.

At the car he got into the back seat and put the bag on his knees, and before I could close the door he put his hand up. He cupped it by his ear, and shook it gently. Then he looked at me with his eyebrows up. My name. Sound. Yes?

"No," I said.

He frowned.

"It isn't Latin," I said. "It's Spanish. Mateo got it wrong. Sana means healthy. It's what a cut does when it closes up." I crouched down by the open door. "It means healing."

He looked at me, and didn't sign anything. Then he reached out and put his fingers back on my throat, as if he was waiting for the rest of it, as if he already knew there was more.

I knelt on the pavement so that his hand could reach without him leaning, and I said it the way I had said it once before, every word the same, and I didn't take any of them back.

"I won't let anything happen to you as long as I am beside you."
